newsitem.title: UK: UK manufacturers cringe at latest rate rise.
newsitem.headline: UK manufacturers cringe at latest rate rise.

text.p: British manufacturers cringed as the Bank of England raised base rates by a quarter-point on Thursday, fearing an even stronger pound will result.

"The general consensus is that the pound will continue to rise...Obviously it is going to harm export prospects further," said John Langley, resident economist at the Engineering Employers' Federation.

The EEF released a survey on Tuesday showing that export orders had fallen to their lowest level for three years. The balance of firms reporting an increase in business fell to minus-10 percent from two percent.
Manufacturers have pointed an accusing finger at sterling which has appreciated more than 20 percent since last August.
"There is the matter of investment as well, a lot of member companies have capital investment projects that are ongoing and it is going to make that harder," Langley said.
But with recent windfall payments from the flotations of various building societies injecting a flood of money into the economy, he said another rate rise may well become necessary.

Ruth Lea, head of the policy unit at the Institute of Directors, agreed sterling was the main problem for policymakers and had some cutting words for Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown's first budget.
"That was a fairly dud budget, if I may say so, and it does not help business," she said.
Following the budget last Wednesday, many analysts said Brown's near six billion pound fiscal tightening plan had not gone far enough to curb buoyant consumer demand.
As a result, many felt it was inevitable that the Bank of England monetary policy committee, empowered by Brown to set interest rates, would announce a rise of at least 25 basis points.
The rise came, sterling fell a pfennig against the mark, but within an hour it was back to its former heights in the region of 2.9650.

Lea said the rate rise had a double-whammy effect on manufacturers. "The second impact is on costs. Higher interest rate costs do not help manufacturers' balance sheets, or indeed businesses' balance sheets in general as their costs will rise."

The hardest hit would be the manufacturers of homogenous products that could be bought elsewhere. Now that the pound had made these goods uncompetitive, buyers would look to manufacturers in other countries.

Neil Blake, research director at Business Strategies Ltd, pointed to the reduction in the Treasury's forecast for manufacturing output growth for this year to 1.5 percent, from the 3.0 percent forecast in the previous budget. That showed the government was aware of the pain caused by sterling's rise, he said.

Sterling was high because it was a safe-haven currency at a time when the prospect of European Monetary Union (EMU) was making most continental currencies somewhat unsteady, Blake said. That was not likely to disappear overnight.
The Confederation of British Industry (CBI) said firms reluctantly accepted the base rate hike.

"Business reluctantly accepts the need for this interest rate rise as last week's budget did not do enough to offset inflationary pressures from domestic demand growth," Adair Turner, director-general at the CBI, said in a statement.
"We would stress that further interest rate rises in the short-term would be unwelcome," he said. "The situation should not be exacerbated and is itself likely to slow growth over the next year."
